article_title: Who Gets the Refund? Brands & Consumers Collide Over Tariffs Windfall
sub_title: The Court of International Trade held that importers of record are entitled to refunds of duties paid under the unlawful tariffs regime.
article_content: More than 2,000 lawsuits have been filed in the wake of the Supreme Court’s February 20 decision striking down emergency tariffs. That ruling not only invalidated tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (“IEEPA”), but it also prompted the U.S. Court of International Trade to recognize that importers of record are entitled to refunds of duties paid under the unlawful tariffs regime. Against that backdrop, companies across industries – and a growing pool of consumers – have moved quickly to recover those sums. In the weeks since the Supreme Court’s decision , the U.S. Court of International Trade’s docket has been flooded with complaints seeking refunds, joining the 1,000-plus cases that were already pending before the Supreme Court issued its opinion. Taken together, the volume of filings reveals both the scale of the financial stakes and the urgency with which companies are moving to secure their part of the estimated $166 billion – plus interest – that U.S. Customs and Border Protection is expected to return. Hundreds of companies across the retail market are among those bringing claims in the post-decision wave, including Jimmy Choo, Versace, Moncler, Stone Island, Marni, Jil Sander, L’Occitane, Byredo, Charlotte Tilbury, Carolina Herrera, Michael Kors, Thom Browne, Maison Margiela, and Good American, among many others. These cases – in which the plaintiffs range from large companies like adidas and Puig to smaller entities like New York-based accessories brand Margaux and B2B resale company LePrix – highlight both the industry-wide impact of the tariffs and the significant sums at issue for brands operating global supply chains. In one such suit , filed on March 17, Skims challenges the government’s assessment of tariffs on its imported merchandise pursuant to executive orders issued under IEEPA, arguing that those duties were unlawful and must be refunded. The claims being lodged by the brand co-founded by Kim Kardashian are not unique. In fact, they closely track those raised across the growing number of complaints being filed by importers, each seeking recovery of duties paid under the now-invalid tariff regime. Like many of those plaintiffs, Skims brings its case as an importer of record that paid tariffs pursuant to a series of 2025 executive orders, relying on the Supreme Court’s decision and related lower court rulings confirming that the IEEPA does not authorize tariffs. Even with the SCOTUS opinion in place , refunds are not automatic. Much of the litigation surge took shape in the immediate aftermath of the decision, before the government launched the Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries (“CAPE”) portal on April 20, creating an administrative path for at least some refund claims. While the portal is being rolled out in phases and does not yet cover every scenario, its launch signals a shift away from a purely litigation-driven recovery process and toward a hybrid model in which companies may pursue refunds through both administrative and judicial channels. The legal landscape is not limited to company-initiated refund actions. A parallel wave of class action litigation has emerged, shifting the focus from managing tariff exposure to managing refund-related risk. In the weeks following the decision, plaintiffs’ firms have begun targeting retailers and consumer-facing companies seeking tariff refunds, advancing the theory that businesses that passed tariff costs on to consumers should not retain the benefit of government reimbursements. As of mid-March, multiple lawsuits reflect a developing argument that such refunds could amount to an impermissible “double recovery.” This evolving risk comes as companies across industries pursue reimbursement of duties paid under the IEEPA regime, arguing that those payments were not legally owed and must be returned with interest. Early post-decision rulings suggest that relief may extend broadly to affected importers, helping to fuel the surge in filings. At the same time, companies that incorporated tariff costs into retail pricing must now consider whether they can defend how those costs were treated if refunds are obtained. As Ballard Spahr’s Stephanie Sheridan and Meegan Brooks recently noted, “hundreds of thousands of importers” could face consumer claims if they receive refunds but cannot demonstrate that they have established a mechanism to return the tariff component of inflated prices to the end consumers who paid them – highlighting the growing legal and financial exposure tied to these claims. THE BIGGER PICTURE : The scope of potential refunds heightens both the opportunity and the exposure for companies across industries, particularly as questions emerge around how tariff-related costs were handled at the consumer level. Although recent lawsuits suggest wide-ranging exposure, many claims may face practical hurdles – especially where pricing decisions cannot be clearly linked to specific tariffs. Even so, the size of potential recoveries is likely to incentivize companies to pursue refunds despite the risk of follow-on litigation. This dynamic forces companies to take a more holistic approach, evaluating not only how to secure refunds but also how to address potential downstream exposure, including through pricing analyses, documentation of cost pass-through, and consideration of consumer-facing remedies. More broadly, trade policy has evolved into a multi-front legal issue, where refund proceedings against the government and private litigation are unfolding in parallel. The addition of an administrative refund mechanism only sharpens that reality, potentially accelerating the return of tariff payments while increasing pressure on companies to justify what happens to those funds once recovered. As a result, companies are no longer simply responding to tariffs – they are navigating the legal and financial consequences of unwinding them. The result? As it becomes easier for companies to recover tariff payments from the government, it may become harder to justify holding onto them. Updated April 20, 2026 This article was initially published in March 20, and has been updated to coincide with the government’s launch of the CAPE portal on April 20. Share

article_title: Fashion Law 2026: The Top U.S. Law Firms for Retail Companies
sub_title: A number of law firms have developed dedicated fashion and retail practices to advise on issues that arise in fashion and consumer goods.
article_content: The fashion business brings with it a highly specific – and increasingly demanding – set of legal considerations. As a specialized, multi-disciplinary legal practice, fashion law spans intellectual property and brand protection , international trade, supply chain oversight, sustainability and ESG compliance , and evolving advertising standards, among other areas, creating a fast-changing regulatory and litigation environment for apparel, luxury, and retail brands. At the same time, the pace of change in the fashion industry shows little sign of slowing. With shifting consumer expectations, emerging technologies, enduring industry consolidation, and ongoing market volatility, companies are increasingly turning to counsel that can offer not only industry fluency, but also practical, business-minded guidance. As a result, a growing number of law firms have developed dedicated fashion and broader retail practices to advise on the issues that arise across the lifecycle of fashion and consumer goods. These firms work closely with brands to mitigate risk, address day-to-day legal needs, and protect the value of both their creative outputs and broader business operations. Against this backdrop, TFL has compiled its second annual list of top law firms working across fashion law, luxury goods, and the wider retail/consumer products sector. In putting together this list, TFL evaluated leading U.S.-based firms with established fashion law practices, considering factors such as the scale and scope of their work, the services they provide, the strength of their client rosters, and their involvement in the fashion law community. The firms are presented in alphabetical order and reflect a cross-section of practices shaping the legal framework of the fashion industry today – from intellectual property portfolio-building and litigation to regulatory compliance, corporate strategy, and beyond. A&O Shearman is a global law firm with over 200 attorneys specializing in the Consumer and Retail industry. The firm provides a comprehensive range of services to its clients, including mergers and acquisitions (M&A), capital markets transactions, financing deals, regulatory matters, commercial agreements, financial restructurings, cybersecurity, data protection, and brand protection. A&O Shearman has been involved in several high-profile financing deals, with clients including Primark, Pandora, Net-a-Porter, Versace, and Etsy. > A&O Shearman’s broad range of services, high-profile clients, and highly regarded M&A practice in the fashion sector position it as a leading fashion law firm. ArentFox Schiff, LLP boasts a robust Fashion & Retail Law practice with over 60 attorneys dedicated to serving the fashion and retail sectors. Their services cover a wide array of areas, including advertising, privacy & data security, e-commerce, class action defense, online distribution & fulfillment, fashion & retail AI, international trade, labor & employment, real estate & leasing, and regulatory, recall & Prop 65. The firm is also highly active in the fashion law community, regularly contributing to industry events and thought leadership. ArentFox Schiff represents a prestigious clientele, including Jimmy Choo, Hugo Boss, Marni, Christian Louboutin, and Balenciaga. > ArentFox Schiff’s extensive team, impressive client roster, firm accolades, and active involvement in the industry underscore its position as a leading fashion law firm. Baker McKenzie is a global law firm with a luxury, fashion, and cosmetics focus. The firm provides expert counsel in brand protection, trade compliance, data privacy, dispute resolution, intellectual property, private M&A, sustainability and ESG, tax for M&A and reorganizations, and cyber risk management. Notable clients include Mytheresa, Capri Holdings, and LVMH, reflecting the firm’s strong foothold in the luxury and fashion sectors, particularly with regard to deal-making. > Baker McKenzie’s recent high-profile deal activity, sizable team, broad service offering, and notable client roster make it a leading fashion law firm. Ballard Spahr LLP is a Philadelphia-based law firm with roots in the fashion and retail law space. The firm’s Retail & E-Commerce practice has significantly expanded following the addition of a four-member litigation team led by Partners Stephanie A. Sheridan and Meegan Brooks, which brought a portfolio of over 100 retail clients. The group advises fashion, beauty, and consumer brands on a broad range of matters, including advertising and marketing compliance, retail and e-commerce issues, intellectual property protection and enforcement, licensing, and regulatory matters affecting consumer-facing businesses. The practice is widely recognized for its consistent strength in the retail sector and longstanding presence in leading industry rankings and directories. > Ballard Spahr’s expanded retail client base and broad range of services for fashion, beauty, and consumer brands underscore its position as a top fashion law firm. Barack Ferrazzano is a Chicago-based firm distinguished for its luxury sector expertise and enduring leadership in fashion law, having represented some of the world’s most prominent luxury brands since 1984. With a dedicated team of attorneys, Barack Ferrazzano offers a comprehensive suite of services encompassing brand and product development, promotion, expansion, sales and distribution, and asset protection. The firm’s multidisciplinary approach also covers corporate law, real estate, intellectual property, employment, litigation, and tax matters. Barack Ferrazzano has established long-standing relationships with iconic brands, notably serving as principal U.S. counsel for the Paris-based LVMH Group. ​ > With decades of experience, an extensive client roster, and recent high-profile deals, Barack Ferrazzano has solidified its status as a leading fashion law firm. Cowan, Liebowitz & Latman (CLL) is a New York-based firm with a long-standing presence at the intersection of intellectual property and fashion, advising brands on how to structure, protect, and scale their businesses across global markets. While best known for its trademark and litigation capabilities, the firm’s work extends into the commercial and operational mechanics of the industry, including distribution, customs, and regulatory compliance. CLL represents a wide range of clients, from emerging labels to established fashion groups, and is particularly active in supporting early-stage designers through educational initiatives, pro bono programs, and academic partnerships. Notable clients include G-III Apparel Group (DKNY, Donna Karan), J.Crew, Lafayette 148, Puig Beauty & Fashion Group (Carolina Herrera, Paco Rabanne, Nina Ricci), Vogue International, Tiffany & Co., Warby Parker, and Zara USA. > CLL’s extensive involvement in the fashion law sector, combined with its focus on brand and product development, promotion, expansion, sales and distribution, and asset protection, makes it a leading fashion law firm. Debevoise & Plimpton is a New York City-based law firm with a team of attorneys experienced in the consumer and retail industry. Their clients include MSCHF, Steve Madden, and StockX. Notably, the firm represented Yves Saint Laurent in a high-profile trademark dispute brought by Christian Louboutin concerning red-soled shoes, successfully defeating Louboutin’s motion for a preliminary injunction. The firm also recently represented The Judd Foundation in a high-profile lawsuit against Kim Kardashian and Clements Design in California federal court involving allegedly inauthentic Donald Judd furniture. With a strong track record in high-stakes intellectual property disputes, Debevoise & Plimpton continues to be a go-to firm for luxury brands seeking to protect and enforce their designs, trademarks, and market positioning and/or to defend against litigation. Debevoise & Plimpton’s attorneys in this practice area are also actively involved in the fashion law community, regularly speaking at industry events and publishing articles on key trends and legal developments. > Debevoise & Plimpton’s recent high-profile litigation and transactional work, along with its longstanding history handling significant fashion intellectual property disputes, establish it as a leading law firm in the fashion and retail space. Dentons is a global law firm with a Luxury, Fashion, and Beauty group comprising a substantial number of attorneys. This group offers an extensive range of services, including licensing, mergers and acquisitions, franchising, employment and labor law, real estate, and more. Dentons has been specializing in luxury, fashion, and beauty for over 40 years. With a strong presence in key fashion hubs worldwide, the firm assists luxury and beauty brands in navigating cross-border transactions, regulatory compliance, and market expansion strategies to stay competitive in a rapidly evolving industry. Some of the firm’s notable clients include Christian Dior Couture, LVMH Group, Sephora USA, Ulta Beauty, Foot Locker, BaubleBar, Dermalogica, and Paula’s Choice. > Dentons is recognized as a leading fashion law firm due to its longstanding Luxury, Fashion, and Beauty practice, extensive global reach, and multidisciplinary capabilities. DLA Piper is a global law firm with a significant presence in the Retail and Fashion sector. Central to its influence is its Trademark, Copyright, and Media practice, through which the firm advises leading brands on trademark portfolio management, brand protection, and false advertising matters. The firm also handles mergers and acquisitions, restructuring, data privacy, real estate, tax, and private equity transactions for fashion and retail clients. DLA Piper maintains an active presence in the fashion and retail law community through industry engagement, speaking roles, and its Consumer Goods, Food & Retail Speaker Series, addressing emerging issues in brand protection, sustainability, and digital commerce. Notable clients include Amazon, Ralph Lauren , Dior, LVMH, Nike, Chanel, H&M, and other prominent fashion and consumer brands. > DLA Piper’s broad global reach, active involvement in the fashion law community, and representation of leading international fashion and retail brands contribute to its status as a leading fashion law firm. Foley & Lardner LLP is a Milwaukee-based law firm with a robust Fashion, Apparel & Beauty (FAB) Industry Team. This interdisciplinary team offers comprehensive legal services to fashion and retail companies, addressing issues ranging from intellectual property to regulatory compliance. Notable clients include Fashion Nova, Puma, Missoni, Steve Madden, TOMS, Carhartt Inc., Christian Dior, and Hermès International. In February 2025, the firm advised Steve Madden in its agreement to acquire UK-based footwear and accessories brand Kurt Geiger. The firm actively engages with the fashion community by publishing industry insights and hosting an annual Fashion Law Year in Review event. > Foley & Lardner’s broad experience in the fashion sector, full-service legal capabilities, representation of prominent brands, and meaningful involvement in industry initiatives firmly establish it as a leading fashion law firm. Fross Zelnick Lehrman & Zissu, P.C. is a New York–based firm known for its deep expertise in intellectual property, particularly within the fashion and luxury sectors. The practice is widely regarded for guiding leading brands through the full lifecycle of trademark strategy – from clearance and registration to enforcement and high-stakes litigation – while also advising on global portfolio management and anti-counterfeiting initiatives. Its client roster includes Aritzia, Gap, Louis Vuitton, David Yurman, Stella McCartney, and Gucci. The firm has built a reputation for handling complex cross-border disputes, domain name conflicts, and copyright issues, helping fashion companies safeguard brand equity and preserve market distinction. > Fross Zelnick’s deep specialization in intellectual property, combined with its representation of leading luxury and fashion brands, establishes it as a premier fashion law firm. Gibney, Anthony & Flaherty, LLP is a New York-based firm that operates at the core of brand protection strategy for fashion and luxury companies, with a practice centered on the development, maintenance, and enforcement of intellectual property rights. The firm works closely with clients on building and managing global trademark portfolios, navigating oppositions and cancellations, and addressing infringement across both traditional retail channels and online marketplaces. In an environment increasingly shaped by cross-border commerce and digital brand exposure, Gibney’s work reflects a steady focus on the operational side of IP, ensuring that protection mechanisms keep pace with how brands are actually marketed, sold, and consumed. > Gibney’s strong intellectual property practice, including its recent work managing luxury trademark portfolios and handling enforcement matters, highlights its standing as a leading fashion law firm. Gibson Dunn is a multinational law firm with a robust Consumer Products & Retail Practice group, encompassing a multidisciplinary bench across intellectual property, privacy, employment, regulatory, and IP transactions. The firm provides strategic legal counsel to clients in the fashion, luxury goods, and retail industries, including trademark enforcement, anti-counterfeiting, data privacy and cybersecurity, FTC advertising and regulatory compliance, labor and employment matters, and intellectual property transactions. With extensive experience handling complex, high-stakes disputes and cross-border matters, Gibson Dunn is widely recognized for advising leading global brands on both litigation and commercial strategy. Notable clients include Christian Dior, Louis Vuitton, Nike, Abercrombie & Fitch, adidas, Fabletics, Zara USA, Vera Wang, Estée Lauder, Milk Makeup, Huda Beauty, Saks, and Crocs. > The firm’s extensive services, impressive client roster, and industry accolades underscore its status as one of the top fashion law firms.​ Greenberg Traurig, LLP is a multinational law firm with a substantial Retail Group. The firm offers a wide range of services, including data privacy and cybersecurity, global supply chain management, distribution and fulfillment, international trade compliance, labor and employment, intellectual property protection, and real estate transactions. Notable clients include Marquee Brands, SHEIN, Keds LLC, and Chico’s FAS. In early 2025, Greenberg Traurig served as legal counsel to Marquee Brands in its acquisition of the home, fashion, and lifestyle brand Laura Ashley. > The firm’s substantial team and recent representation of notable clients in high-profile transactions highlight its prominence in the fashion law sector. Hogan Lovells is an international firm co-headquartered in London and Washington, DC. It boasts a well-established fashion and luxury practice, advising brands across a broad spectrum of legal and regulatory issues. Its team counsels clients on intellectual property strategy, data privacy, sustainability compliance, supply chain oversight, and brand enforcement, alongside navigating the complexities of global trade and digital retail. The firm represents a range of high-profile clients, including Gucci, Pandora, Sotheby’s, Supergoop!, and Neil Lane. Known for its cross-border capabilities, Hogan Lovells delivers integrated, end-to-end guidance to fashion and luxury companies operating within an increasingly regulated and digitally driven marketplace. > Hogan Lovells’ extensive fashion practice, deep roster of high-profile clients, and broad engagement across industry initiatives reinforce its leading position in the fashion law sector. Jayaram Law is a boutique law firm with a fashion and art law focus. The firm specializes in intellectual property, data privacy, and corporate growth matters. In 2025, the firm launched Creative Legal Alliance, a pro bono fellowship supporting creatives in the fashion and art worlds. In addition to its Creative Legal Alliance initiative, the firm is actively engaged in the broader fashion law community through its biannual magazine, development of a Sneaker Law textbook, and academic contributions by its attorneys. Some of the firm’s notable clients include Aimé Leon Dore, Chanel, Louis Vuitton, MSCHF, KidSuper, Daniel Arsham Studio, Eberjey, Perry Ellis, Barragán, Bossi, Entire Studios, Hidden.NY, Homerun NYC, House of Errors, PALY Hollywood, Satisfy, Siegelman + Stable, Sushi Club, and Veneda Carter. > Jayaram’s specialization in intellectual property and extensive involvement in the fashion law community make it a top fashion law firm.​ K&L Gates maintains a global Consumer Goods & Services practice that brings together attorneys across its international offices to advise fashion and luxury clients. The Pittsburgh-headquartered firm offers multidisciplinary counsel spanning intellectual property, regulatory compliance, real estate, M&A, technology, data protection, and international trade. Its team regularly guides brands on the legal dimensions of digital commerce, including privacy frameworks for online retail and coordinated anti-counterfeiting strategies, positioning clients to operate effectively across increasingly complex and cross-border markets. > The firm’s large practice group, deep engagement in the fashion law community through industry events and programming, and broad full-service capabilities position it as a leading fashion law firm. Katten Muchin Rosenman LLP , headquartered in Chicago, is a global firm with a dedicated focus on the fashion, retail, luxury, and beauty sectors. Its multidisciplinary group advises clients across a wide range of matters, including M&A and corporate transactions, ESG-related disputes and sustainability compliance, intellectual property, litigation, and trademark strategy and licensing. The firm also brings significant experience in anti-counterfeiting, supporting brands in enforcing their rights across both physical and digital channels. Beyond its client work, Katten remains active in the broader fashion law ecosystem, frequently spearheading industry programming and initiatives. Its client roster includes Aeropostale, Authentic Brands Group, Brooks Brothers, Calvin Klein, Charlotte Tilbury, Kenneth Cole, Kith, Marc Jacobs International, and PVH Corp. > Katten’s broad service offerings, high-profile client roster, recognized industry accolades, and standout individual attorneys in the space collectively solidify its position as a leading fashion law firm. Kelley Drye & Warren LLP a New York-based firm with a well-established role advising fashion and retail companies on regulatory risk and compliance, particularly as scrutiny around marketing, sustainability, and consumer protection continues to intensify. The firm’s practice spans advertising law, product safety, international trade, and litigation, with a notable emphasis on helping brands substantiate claims and navigate evolving FTC guidance and ESG-related expectations. As regulatory frameworks around “green” marketing, data use, and consumer disclosures become more defined and more actively enforced, Kelley Drye has positioned itself as a go-to firm for companies seeking to align business practices with shifting legal standards. The firm is also active in the fashion law community, hosting an annual Fashion and Retail Law Summit. Notable clients include Cult Gaia, Gucci, and Polo Ralph Lauren. > The breadth of services offered to esteemed fashion clients highlights the firm’s prominence in the fashion law sector.​​ Kilpatrick Townsend & Stockton LLP Kilpatrick Townsend & Stockton LLP is an Atlanta-based firm with a strong foothold in intellectual property, advising fashion and consumer brands on the protection and enforcement of trademarks, copyrights, and trade dress across global markets. The firm is particularly active in handling disputes and portfolio strategy for companies operating at scale, where brand identity and product differentiation are central to market position. Kilpatrick Townsend is actively involved in the fashion law community, contributing thought leadership through journal articles and participating in industry initiatives. Notable clients include adidas, Tory Burch, Macy’s, Hugo Boss, Rothy’s, PVH Corp. (Calvin Klein, Tommy Hilfiger), and Oxford Industries (Tommy Bahama, Lilly Pulitzer, Johnny Was). > The firm’s prominent client roster and active involvement in the fashion law community underscore its status as a leading fashion law firm.​ Knobbe Martens , headquartered in Irvine, California, is an intellectual property-focused firm with a dedicated Fashion & Beauty practice that centers on protecting the creative and technical assets underlying modern fashion brands. The firm’s work spans trademarks, trade dress, copyrights, patents, and unfair competition, with an emphasis on helping clients secure and enforce rights tied to both design and innovation. As fashion companies increasingly intersect with technology, whether through product development, materials, or branding, Knobbe Martens’ capabilities reflect a broader view of IP that goes beyond traditional trademark work. Notable clients include Kate Spade, Hurley International, Olaplex, Oakley, and Rolex, reflecting the firm’s strong presence in the luxury sector. Its client base underscores its role in advising brands on how to safeguard distinctiveness in a crowded and fast-moving market. > With a comprehensive service offering and prominent client roster, Knobbe Martens stands out as a leading fashion law firm, providing strategic legal solutions to protect and enhance clients’ brands and products. Loeb & Loeb LLP operates within the retail industry, with a team of attorneys based in New York and Los Angeles. The firm’s attorneys are frequent speakers at fashion and beauty law summits worldwide. It assists clients with brand protection, advertising and marketing, privacy and data, fintech, corporate and transactional matters, consumer litigation and regulatory issues, outsourcing, and real estate transactions. Notable clients include Bergdorf Goodman, Canada Goose, Farm Rio, Furla, Ganni, Golden Goose, Lanvin, Marco Bicego, Moncler, Neiman Marcus, Saint Laurent, and Stella McCartney. Loeb & Loeb is nationally and internationally recognized in the fashion law field, advising on influencer marketing regulations, intellectual property disputes, sustainability compliance, and digital commerce. The firm’s strength in entertainment and media further supports high-profile brand collaborations, licensing agreements, and sponsorship deals for luxury fashion houses. > The firm’s extensive activity in the fashion law community, high-profile client list, and broad range of services underscore its status as one of the top fashion law firms.​ Morgan, Lewis & Bockius LLP is a global law firm with dedicated Luxury & Fashion Brands and Retail & E-Commerce capabilities. The firm advises its retail clients on a broad range of matters, including commercial contracts, private equity and M&A transactions, intellectual property, data protection and privacy compliance, regulatory compliance, disputes and litigation, and labor and employment matters. Morgan Lewis also handles cutting edge issues like influencer marketing and AI regulations. Morgan Lewis attorneys are active in the retail industry and regularly participate in seminars and programming addressing brand protection and industry developments. Clients include Gap Inc. and URBN. > Morgan Lewis’s global reach, firm engagement in the fashion law community, and comprehensive full-service intellectual property, regulatory, and commercial offerings position it as a leading fashion law firm. Morrison Cohen LLP , a New York-based law firm, launched its Luxury Brands practice in the summer of 2024. The group advises clients on bankruptcy, restructuring and governance, business litigation, corporate transactions, executive compensation and employee benefits, labor and employment, real estate, technology, data, and intellectual property. The firm’s notable clients include Valentino, Moncler, OTB, Diesel, Zimmermann, Camilla, and Dion Lee. In 2025, the group successfully beat a class certification bid against Valentino in a wage and hour lawsuit. > The firm’s comprehensive service offerings and recent involvement in high-profile litigation underscore its standing as a leading fashion law firm in the U.S. ​ Norton Rose Fulbright is a global law firm with a significant presence in the luxury and fashion industries. Notable clients include G-III Apparel Group and Donna Karan. > ​The firm’s global presence, comprehensive legal services, and involvement in the fashion law community make it a leading fashion law firm. The firm also recently represented Ralph Lauren Corporation in its $500 million notes offering. > The firm’s achievements in fashion law, prestigious client base, and recent high-profile transactions in the space highlight its status as a leading fashion law firm. Notable clients include Amazon, Arc’teryx, Costco, Crocs, J.Crew, Lululemon, Nordstrom, REI, and Starbucks. > Perkins Coie’s robust Retail & Consumer Products practice, extensive roster of leading apparel and lifestyle brands, and broad full-service capabilities position it as a leading fashion law firm. Pryor Cashman LLP is a New York-based law firm with a dedicated Fashion Group. The firm offers a comprehensive range of services to fashion clients, including corporate formation, real estate transactions, joint ventures and partnership agreements, mergers and acquisitions, contract drafting, labor and employment, and immigration. Notable clients include Richemont, Gucci America, Inc., Camuto Group, Jimmy Choo, Prada, and Cartier North America. In addition to traditional corporate and transactional matters, the firm provides strategic counsel on intellectual property protection, brand enforcement, licensing agreements, and anti-counterfeiting measures to safeguard the creative assets of luxury fashion houses. > Pryor Cashman LLP’s dedicated Fashion Group, strong representation of leading luxury brands, and full-spectrum capabilities position it as a top domestic fashion law firm. Ropes & Gray LLP is a multinational law firm with a strong Consumer & Retail Brands practice. The firm advises fashion, luxury, and consumer brands on a broad range of matters, including strategic transactions, intellectual property protection and licensing, employment issues, and data privacy and cybersecurity, with particular strength in supporting branded consumer businesses across their operations. Notable clients include adidas, Marquee Brands, Luxury Brand Partners (In Common, IGK, R+CO, Smith & Cult), and TJX Companies. The firm is also consistently recognized for its highly-regarded trademark practice and presence in leading industry rankings, underscoring its strong position in the retail and consumer products space. > Ropes & Gray’s strong brand management practice and long-standing work with consumer brands highlight its status as a leading fashion law firm. Rothwell Figg is a DC-based law firm with over three decades of experience in the high fashion and beauty space. Leveraging its expertise in intellectual property, litigation, and technology law, the firm advises clients on a wide range of matters, including copyright registration. In 2025, the firm represented YOOX Net-a-Porter in a patent troll case. Some of the firm’s notable clients include Bvlgari, Chanel, Giuseppe Zanotti, Hoodrich, Shiseido Americas, Stella McCartney, and Valentino. > Rothwell Figg’s deep expertise in intellectual property and litigation, its representation of prominent clients, and active involvement in the fashion law community position it as a leading firm in the fashion law sector. Sheppard Mullin Richter & Hampton LLP is a multinational firm with a substantial Retail, Fashion & Beauty practice. The firm advises fashion industry clients on various matters, including litigation, labor and employment, securing and enforcing patents, trademarks, and copyrights, both domestically and internationally, and handling technology transfers, including assignments, licensing, and joint ventures. The firm represented Chanel in its win against What Goes Around Comes Around, with other notable clients including Nordstrom, Burberry, Levi Strauss, Kate Spade, and Patagonia. > The firm’s longstanding relationships with leading luxury brands and record of significant legal victories affirm its status as one of the top fashion law firms. The Fashion Law’s Top Fashion Law Firms™ ranking is based on a rigorous evaluation process by The Fashion Law’s editorial team. TFL conducts independent research and analysis, including an extensive examination of publicly available information to determine a firm’s standing within the fashion law space. The review and ranking process also takes into account voluntary law firm submissions detailing practice focus, market reputation, client impact, and firm commitment, which are assessed and fact-checked by TFL. Eligibility Firms with five or more lawyers in their U.S. fashion practice are eligible to receive a ranking. Because fashion practices are not always explicitly labeled as such, this list also includes firms with dedicated practices in fashion, retail, luxury, consumer goods, or related areas where the firm demonstrates significant work representing fashion clients. Submission Process As part of the research process, a submission survey was publicly distributed for completion by law firms. The voluntary survey requested information on each firm’s fashion-related practice, including confidential client and litigation details that may not be publicly available and are, therefore, not detailed in the ranking. The survey gathered information across four main areas: practice focus, market reputation, client impact, and firm commitment. (Note: Not all firms on the ranking submitted information in response to the survey.) Evaluation Criteria The Fashion Law’s team primarily engaged in external research across these core categories (Practice Focus; Market Reputation; Client Impact; Firm Commitment; and Notable Practitioners) to determine the inclusion of firms on the 2026 ranking. The team also evaluated any voluntary survey submissions. Share

article_title: Exiting Chapter 11, Pat McGrath Labs Looks to Scalable Growth
sub_title: Pat McGrath Labs is exiting Chapter 11 with fresh capital, a cleaned-up balance sheet, and a more defined path forward.
article_content: Pat McGrath Labs is exiting Chapter 11 with fresh capital, a cleaned-up balance sheet, and a more defined path forward, aiming to turn its creative clout into a business that can operate – and scale – with greater consistency. The move follows its January filing in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Florida, where the brand disclosed more than $50 million in liabilities. Halting a lender-led sale process, the 11-year-old company pursued a restructuring aimed at stabilizing the business and securing new funding. Backed by more than $65 million in financing from GDA Luma, New York-headquartered Pat McGrath labs said its court-approved restructuring “provides a strong foundation for a new phase of creative excellence, operational discipline, innovation-led growth, and sustainable long-term success.” As part of that reset, the prestige beauty brand has invested in its supply chain and commercial operations to better manage inventory and execution – two areas that tend to determine whether early momentum translates into sustainable growth. At the same time, the company says that it has reinforced ties with retail and vendor partners, citing “accelerating sales trends” and “improving retail performance” as early signs that the business is stabilizing. The post-restructuring ownership structure signals a shift in control and governance. GDA Luma will take a controlling equity stake and work to “stabilize the foundation of the business” and implement “best-in-class operating disciplines,” underscoring a broader pattern in the prestige beauty space: investor-led recalibration of brands built on outsized creative equity but challenged by the operational demands of global scale. Still, the company is leaning heavily on the asset that made it relevant in the first place. Founder Pat McGrath will remain Chief Creative Officer, continuing to “push boundaries” as the brand looks to pair its editorial authority with a more structured commercial strategy. The bet, in effect, is that creative credibility – when matched with tighter execution – can be converted into durable, long-term growth. From Resale to Saks’ Restructuring: Inside Chanel’s Exercise in Brand Control
sub_title: Few legal battles have spotlighted this balance more than Chanel v. The RealReal, the closely watched resale case.
article_content: The business of luxury hinges as much on product as it does on the carefully constructed ecosystem of image-making, exclusivity, and control that underpins how brands operate. Few legal battles have spotlighted this balance more than Chanel v. The RealReal , the closely watched resale case that was filed suit back in 2018. What initially appeared to center on allegations of counterfeiting and false advertising has evolved into a broader reflection of Chanel’s global strategy , one defined by the principle that even genuine products, when sold or marketed under the wrong conditions, can threaten the integrity of a luxury brand. It is against that backdrop that Chanel is taking on The RealReal. Its claims go beyond the sale of allegedly inauthentic goods, with the luxury giant arguing that The RealReal has engaged in marketing practices that create a false impression of affiliation, including statements about its “authentication experts” and the use of Chanel trademarks in connection with product listings and promotions. According to Chanel, these practices constitute infringement and deception, even when the goods themselves are authentic. The RealReal has pushed back from the outset, characterizing the suit as a “thinly-veiled effort” to eliminate resale competition and to prevent consumers from accessing Chanel products at lower price points. Chanel’s case against The RealReal is part of a larger, ongoing legal campaign. Across cases in the U.S., the U.K., and Europe, Chanel has taken the position that resale of genuine goods, when conducted outside of approved channels or conditions, poses a reputational risk. That argument was recently validated in by Chanel v. What Goes Around Comes Around (“WGACA”), which resulted in a significant win for the brand in 2025. Following a jury trial and subsequent bench trial on equitable remedies, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York issued a final judgment broadly siding with Chanel. A federal jury found the reseller liable for willful trademark infringement and false advertising after it sold handbags linked to stolen serial numbers and engaged in marketing that suggested affiliation with Chanel. The court ordered WGACA to pay $4 million in statutory damages and more than $500,000 in litigation costs. Crucially, the court also issued an injunction that bars WGACA from using Chanel’s trademarks – including in hashtags, marketing materials, and visual displays – in any manner that suggests affiliation. It further prohibits the company from making authentication claims about Chanel products unless it possesses independent authentication records to support them. The court’s opinion reaffirmed a core tenet of Chanel’s legal stance: resale may be legal, but it is not a license to piggyback on another company’s branding and goodwill. “The right to resell a genuine product does not give the reseller the right to use the brand owner’s trademarks and other intellectual property in a way that is likely to lead consumers to believe that the brand owner has endorsed, or is somehow associated with, the reseller,” wrote Judge Louis L. Stanton in his June 2025 opinion . The outcome in WGACA – paired with Chanel’s litigation activity in other key markets – reflects a legal strategy grounded in the belief that product authenticity alone is not sufficient. Chanel has worked to ensure that its goods are not only genuine but also sold under conditions that adhere to its carefully managed brand identity. Saks Global’s bankruptcy adds another dimension to Chanel’s broader brand control strategy. In a January 30 letter submitted to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, counsel for Chanel and The RealReal informed the court that they had agreed on a mediation date, but that “scheduling has been complicated by recent developments which have occupied the attention of key decision-makers,” including Chanel’s response to the Saks Global bankruptcy. While Chanel’s recent filing references Saks’ Chapter 11 proceedings only very briefly, its role in the restructuring process is significant. After all, Chanel is not merely a vendor caught in the fallout but one of Saks’ largest unsecured creditors (owed approximately $136 million) and a key party to the newly-formed Official Committee of Unsecured Saks Creditors . The 10-member committee, which includes other luxury suppliers like LVMH and Kering, real estate stakeholders, and Amazon, is tasked with helping to steer Saks’ $3.4 billion restructuring process. Chanel’s position on the committee gives it a direct say in how and to what extent Saks continues to operate in a way that aligns with luxury brand expectations. This dual role, as both supplier and creditor, reflects a broader strategy Chanel has pursued across jurisdictions: asserting control over where and how its products are sold, not just through litigation but also through commercial leverage. As wholesale channels face pressure and department stores restructure, Chanel’s distribution strategy now extends beyond the courtroom to include influence in retail bankruptcies like Saks. As Saks moves forward and reportedly unwinds its e-commerce partnership with Amazon, the split highlights a growing divide between brands and multi-brand retail platforms. Chanel, as a major creditor with a seat on the committee overseeing Saks’ restructuring, will have a say in how the retailer evolves. But it is unclear whether Chanel – or other luxury brands that have been actively scaling back wholesale – still see a long-term future with Saks. As the retailer works to redefine itself, part of the question is whether it can retain its luxury partners. Or put another way, whether those partners still see Saks as the right environment for their brands. THE BOTTOM LINE : With a landmark judgment already in hand from the WGACA case (and courts in Europe endorsing strict enforcement over the resale of luxury goods), Chanel appears well-positioned to continue shaping the legal boundaries of how its goods are marketed and resold. Whether or not its case against The RealReal is resolved through mediation, the broader message is clear: Chanel is determined to assert control over how its products are sold, even long after they have left the boutique.
